name: Ming
lede: Ming is a deep, greyed greenish-blue named for the Chinese dynasty and its porcelain, though the porcelain's famous blue was cobalt, a different and more violet color.

sections.title: What the word points to
sections.body:
In color dictionaries *Ming* is an adjective for a hue used in making Ming porcelain, as in Ming blue and Ming green [3]. The dynasty itself ruled China from 1368, and books give slightly different end dates: 1642 in Paterson's dictionary, 1643 in Balfour-Paul's study of indigo [3][2]. The name therefore points at a whole era of glazes and enamels, not at one recipe, and who first used it as a plain color name is undocumented in our sources.

The archive of named colors files Ming as a dark blue with a faint green lean, a near neighbor of [[teal-blue]] and [[genoa-blue]] [5][7]. It appears in the ISCC-NBS lists of 1955, in block 141 (the block that also holds a different color, Ming Green, which the same list places among the viridian-like greens) [5].

sections.title: Blue from Persia
sections.body:
The great blue of Ming porcelain was not made in China at first [1]. Finlay reports that for some four hundred years the Chinese swapped green [[celadon]] ware for [[cobalt]] blue from Persia, and the Persians had learned to use cobalt as a glaze long before [1]. He describes cobalt as a costly blue that leans toward violet [1], which is why the swatch here, greener and greyer, is only a distant cousin of the porcelain blue.

The cobalt did not stay constant. Finlay, working from notes at the Victoria and Albert Museum, places the finest blue in the Xuande reign, around the middle of the 1400s, while under the Zhengde and Jiajing emperors a century later makers used an excellent violet glaze [1]. He adds that the blue-and-white of the late Chenghua and Wanli reigns was nearly grey and white after trade sanctions against Central Asia, though he flags the dates as awkward himself [1]. By his account a visitor can then tell roughly when a Ming vase was fired by its color alone [1].

The blue also traveled into cloth. Balfour-Paul notes that rugs made in China during the Ming dynasty consciously echoed the blue designs of the porcelain, and that Chinese export blue-and-white later helped sustain a European taste for indigo prints [2].

sections.title: Greens, enamels and rank
sections.body:
Ming color was not only blue. Paterson defines the Five Colours as Ming-era porcelain decorated with enamels in apple green, aubergine, iron red, violet and yellow [3]. Green pigment appears on Ming walls too: the Pigment Compendium records [[malachite]] identified on Ming wall paintings in central China [8].

Color also marked status. Finlay writes that the Qing inherited the Ming examination system and the Ming practice of marking rank with an embroidered mandarin square, a bird for civil officials and an animal for army officers [4]. In the Qing code he describes, blue-black silk indicated a civil servant [4].

sections.title: The swatch is not the vase
sections.body: Our swatch is a measured screen color, not a glaze. Its nearest standard name among our paint-and-pigment colors is [[teal]], about 7.7 units away in CIEDE2000 [5]. A real Ming blue-and-white vase, a cobalt blue that leans toward violet, would sit noticeably bluer than this [1]. Treat the name as a label for an era, not a recipe.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 47 works, and it appears in 86 under the looser test of the color-name lens [6]. It is rarer than 56 per cent of the named colors [6]. Inside a painting it is most often a hidden color, a quiet mid-tone rather than an accent: 62 per cent of the 32 paintings measured by lightness rank [6].

The earliest match is a 1445 painting by Domenico Veneziano, [[painting:nga-362|a panel by Domenico Veneziano]], the earliest of 58 dated paintings with at least two per cent coverage [6]. That is 510 years before the name's first record in our sources (1955), so the match is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof of a pigment [6]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, so read them as screen colors [6].

origin.named_after: the Ming dynasty (1368 to the 1640s) and its porcelain
origin.first_recorded: ISCC-NBS 1955 (as a color name in our sources); the porcelain sense is older and undocumented
origin.source: Paterson, A Dictionary of Colour; ColorHub library

disambiguation.gloss: Ming Green is a separate, much greener ISCC-NBS name filed beside viridian

questions.q: In Finlay's account, what did China send to Persia in exchange for cobalt blue?
True or false: the blue on Ming porcelain stayed the same color throughout the dynasty.
Which of these belongs to the Five Colours of Ming enamel decoration?

openers: The famous Ming blue was cobalt from Persia, and its shade changed from reign to reign.
Ming porcelain was also painted in five enamel colors, among them apple green and aubergine.

issues: Claims verified against fact card and book text; no fixes needed.
